issues.item: Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
issues.explanation: For a 56-year-old combat pilot whose index trauma is a life-threatening accident, the trigger set is dominated by bodily-state cues (dizziness, feeling ill), which fits accident-related threat. 'Other people expressing anger, even calmly' points instead toward an interpersonal/assault schema and is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, especially given the absence of other social-conflict or perpetrator-related items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies pervasive interpersonal mistrust. In this profile, the appraisals otherwise center on emotional deadness and a shattered worldview after accident trauma. Strong distrust of others is possible, but here it lacks support from the trigger/threat/memory pattern and feels mismatched with a non-interpersonal accident presentation.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm' conflicts with the rest of the threat profile, which is strongly hypervigilant and danger-sensitive (body on alert, startle to movement) and with avoidance-based coping. While some trauma survivors do engage in risk taking, this specific item sits awkwardly in a profile otherwise organized around fear, somatic triggering, and withdrawal, without corroborating disinhibition or anger-driven strategies.

vignette:
Thomas, a 56-year-old European American combat pilot, came to treatment after a long stretch of trying to outrun the aftermath of a life-threatening accident that occurred during a routine flight training mission. He had been handling a high-performance aircraft when a sudden mechanical failure and explosive bang jolted the cockpit; the plane dropped sharply, warning lights flashed, and for a few terrifying moments he was sure he would not get the aircraft back under control. He survived, but in the weeks that followed he found that even ordinary bodily sensations could carry him back to that day. If he felt dizzy or lightheaded on standing, or if he came down with a flu-like sense of feeling physically unwell, his mind immediately went to the cockpit and the brief, sickening loss of control. The same happened with sharp bangs in the environment - a slammed door in the hangar, a backfire from a vehicle, even an unexpected pop on a television program - each sound struck him as though danger were already in the room. In those moments his body became tense and ready to react, and he found himself scanning his surroundings, startled by movement near him as if every quick gesture might signal an emergency.

What unsettled Thomas most was not only the sensations themselves but what they seemed to prove. He had come to believe that the world was dangerous, that the assumptions he had built his life on had been shattered, and that something in him had died that day. He described feeling dead inside, as if the accident had hollowed out the part of him that once felt steady and purposeful. That conviction made the triggering sensations even more ominous: dizziness no longer felt like a passing physical symptom, but like evidence that catastrophe could return at any moment; a bang did not just remind him of the accident, it confirmed his belief that the world could turn lethal without warning. He had always trusted training, procedure, and control, and after the accident he felt those beliefs were completely destroyed. His sense that danger was everywhere made him wary of his own body, and his own numbness seemed to him like proof that he was not the same man who had once flown confidently and lived with a sense of mastery.

Over the months that followed, Thomas began arranging his life around the need to feel safe and in control. He avoided hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations whenever he could, even when his wife urged him to get checked after minor illnesses. He gave up pleasant activities he used to enjoy, not because he no longer wanted them, but because enjoyment itself felt irresponsible and exposed, as though letting his guard down would invite another disaster. He also began restricting his eating strictly, telling himself that controlling food was one domain in which he could still impose order on a body that had otherwise become unreliable. Yet the more he tried to manage things this way, the more his mind returned to the accident and the more certain he became that the world truly was dangerous. Each avoidance choice seemed to confirm that there was something to fear: if hospitals and examinations were unbearable, maybe there really was a hidden problem in his body; if he had to micromanage food to feel steady, maybe he could not trust himself at all. That inward conclusion deepened his emotional numbness and his shattered beliefs, making it harder to imagine any future that did not revolve around vigilance and loss.

At the same time, those habits kept his body on alert. By narrowing his world, he found himself watching himself more closely, bracing for the next dizzy spell, the next bang, the next sudden movement near him. The effort of staying guarded was exhausting, and the tension never fully left his muscles. He noticed it at work in the flight operations environment, where the noise of equipment, quick motion on the tarmac, and emergency vehicles crossing nearby would jolt him into instant alarm. Instead of easing with familiarity, his alarm made him more determined to avoid medical settings and any situation that might remind him of vulnerability. His wife had begun to notice that he declined dinners, skipped golf with friends, and grew terse whenever someone suggested a checkup. What started as an attempt to protect himself had become a pattern that kept reinforcing the very world he feared: the more he avoided, the more dangerous everything felt, and the more threatening his own reactions became. It was this tightening cycle, along with a recent episode of dizziness that sent him into a panic when he heard an ambulance outside the base clinic, that finally brought him to seek help. Thomas said he was most afraid that he had become permanently trapped in a life of hyperalertness and emotional emptiness, but he was also quietly hoping that treatment might help him feel safe in his own body again and reclaim some sense that the world was not entirely ruined.
